questions.question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.
Throw one into a quandary.

options.text: To plead with someone, especially a figure of authority, to show one lenience and mercy
To cause one to become unsure, confused, or perplexed about the best course of action
To shock, surprise, astonish, or bewilder one
To put one in the position to be the recipient of blame, trouble, or criticism, often that which was intended for oneself.

questions.solution: The correct answer is **Option(2)** i.e. **'To cause one to become unsure, confused, or perplexed about the best course of action'**. **__Key Points__** __ • The idiom **'Throw one into a quandary'** refers to a situation where someone is placed in a state of perplexity, uncertainty, or a difficult dilemma where the best course of action is not clear. (असमंजस या दुविधा में डालना) • **Example: **The sudden resignation of the CEO **threw the entire board into a quandary** regarding the future of the company. • To **'cause one to become unsure, confused, or perplexed'** means to create a state of mental uncertainty or bewilderment, making it difficult for a person to decide what to do next. (किसी को भ्रमित या अनिश्चित करना) • **Example: **The complex and contradictory technical requirements **caused the engineers to become perplexed** during the planning phase. • Hence, the meaning of the idiom aligns perfectly with the description of being confused or unsure about a course of action. Therefore, the correct answer is- **To cause one to become unsure, confused, or perplexed about the best course of action**. **Additional Information__** Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences: • **To plead with someone** (दया की याचना करना या विनती करना): To beg or request someone, especially an authority figure, for mercy or leniency. • **Example:** The student had to **plead with the professor** for an extension on his final project. • **To shock, surprise, astonish, or bewilder one** (स्तब्ध या चकित कर देना): To cause a sudden feeling of intense surprise or disbelief. • **Example:** The magician's final trick **astonished the entire audience**. • **To put one in the position to be the recipient of blame** (किसी पर दोष मढ़ना या बलि का बकरा बनाना): To make someone else responsible for a mistake or criticism, often to protect oneself. • **Example:** He tried to **put his teammate in the position to be the recipient of blame** for the loss, even though it was his own error. 36:Tc5e, The correct answer is: **By an extremely slim or narrow margin**.

questions.question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.
By a short head.

options.text: By an extremely slim or narrow margin
To lack enough people to do something easily, efficiently, or effectively, usually because some of the usual participants are unavailable
By a particular amount of something, especially points in a game or contest, over or below another amount

questions.solution: The correct answer is: **By an extremely slim or narrow margin**. **__Key Points__** __ • The idiom **'By a short head'** refers to winning or succeeding by a very small distance or margin, originally derived from **horse racing** where a winner might only be ahead by the length of its head. (बहुत कम अंतर से) • **Example:** The incumbent mayor won the re-election **by a short head** after a very competitive campaign. • **'By an extremely slim or narrow margin'** means a situation where the difference between two outcomes is very tiny or minimal. (बहुत ही मामूली अंतर से) • **Example:** The bill was passed in the parliament **by an extremely slim margin** of only three votes. • Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'By a short head'** is to win or lose by a very small amount. Therefore, the correct answer is- **By an extremely slim or narrow margin**. **Additional Information__** Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences: • **To lack enough people** (कर्मियों की कमी होना): This is often described by the idiom **'short-handed'**, meaning not having enough staff or help. • **Example:** The kitchen was **short-handed** on Saturday night, so the service was slower than usual. • **A hangover** (खुमारी): The unpleasant physical and mental effects experienced after drinking too much alcohol. • **Example:** He spent the entire Sunday in bed trying to recover from a terrible **hangover**. • **By a particular amount** (एक विशेष मात्रा या अंतर से): Referring to a specific numerical value or score that separates two entities in a competition. • **Example:** They trailed the leaders **by a particular amount** of points that made a comeback nearly impossible. 37:Tac6, The correct answer is: **Egregious**.

A person who behaves in an unconventional manner.

• **Example: **The **eccentric** billionaire preferred living in a small cabin in the woods rather than a luxury mansion.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
Will the sponsors invite the whole team to the party?

options.text: Will the whole team invite to the party by the sponsors?
Will the whole team invite the sponsors to the party?
Will the whole team been invited to the party by the sponsors?
Will the whole team be invited to the party by the sponsors?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Will the whole team be invited to the party by the sponsors?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is an **interrogative sentence** written in the **Future Indefinite Tense** (Active Voice). It denotes an inquiry about a future action.

• The structure for an **interrogative sentence** in the **Active Voice** (Simple Future) is: **Will/Shall + Subject + Root Form of Verb (V1) + Object?** In the prompt, **the sponsors** is the subject and **the whole team** is the object.

• To convert such a sentence into **Passive Voice**, the structure must change to: **Will/Shall + Object (New Subject) + be + Past Participle (V3) + by + Subject (New Object)?**

• Following this rule, the **object** 'the whole team' is moved to the position of the subject. The **auxiliary verb** 'be' is added before the **past participle** form of the verb 'invite', which is **invited**.

• The original subject 'the sponsors' is placed at the end of the clause, preceded by the preposition **by** to indicate the **agent** of the action.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Rules of Passive Transformation**:

• For **Future Indefinite** sentences, the addition of the word **be** is mandatory to support the **third form of the verb**.

• The **tense** of the sentence must remain consistent during the transformation; only the focus shifts from the **doer** to the **receiver** of the action.

• If the sentence were a declarative statement (e.g., 'The sponsors will invite...'), the passive would be 'The whole team **will be invited**...'.

• Evaluation of Incorrect Options:

• **Option 1** is incorrect because it uses the **first form** of the verb 'invite' and completely omits the required auxiliary **be**.

• **Option 2** is incorrect because it maintains the **Active Voice** structure while simply swapping the positions of the subject and object, which fundamentally alters the **intended meaning**.

• **Option 3** is incorrect as it uses **been**. This auxiliary is exclusively used for **Perfect Tenses** (like Future Perfect: 'will have been invited') and is not used in Simple Future passive structures.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
They were felicitating war veterans at the event.

options.text: War veterans were felicitated at the event.
War veterans are being felicitated at the event.
War veterans were felicitating at the event.
War veterans were being felicitated at the event.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**War veterans were being felicitated at the event**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is in the **Active Voice** and follows the **Past Continuous Tense** structure: **Subject + was/were + Verb-ing + Object**.

• To convert a **Past Continuous** sentence into **Passive Voice**, the following rule is applied: **New Subject (Object of Active) + was/were + being + V3 (Past Participle) + by + New Object (Subject of Active)**.

• In the original sentence, **They** is the subject, **were felicitating** is the verb, and **war veterans** is the object.

• When transformed, **war veterans** becomes the new subject. Since it is plural, the auxiliary verb **were** is used, followed by **being** and the third form of the verb **felicitated**.

• The phrase **at the event** remains as an adverbial adjunct at the end of the sentence.

 **Additional Information__**

• Understanding why other options are grammatically unsuitable for this transformation:

• **Simple Past Passive**: Option 1 uses **were felicitated**, which is the structure for the **Simple Past Tense** in passive voice (S + was/were + V3). It fails to convey the continuous nature of the original action.

• **Present Continuous Passive**: Option 2 uses **are being felicitated**, which changes the tense from **Past** to **Present**, thereby altering the temporal context of the original statement.

• **Meaning Discrepancy**: Option 3 suggests that the **war veterans** themselves were performing the action of felicitating others, which changes the intended meaning of the active sentence entirely.

</ul

questions.question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives (A), (B), (C), and (D). There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence that has the error. Choosing the alternative with the error will be the answer.
Nirmala has a passion in writing one-act plays based on realities, and she is really adept at it.

options.text: Nirmala has a passion in writing

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the first part of the sentence: **Nirmala has a passion in writing**.
 
• The noun **passion** is typically followed by the preposition **for** when referring to a strong liking or enthusiasm for a particular activity or subject.
 
• Therefore, the phrase **passion in writing** is grammatically incorrect and should be replaced with **passion for writing**.
 
• Using the correct prepositional idiom is essential for clarity and standard grammatical usage in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'Nirmala has a **passion for writing** one-act plays based on realities, and she is really adept at it.'*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **one-act plays based on realities** – This part is correct. **One-act** is a compound adjective modifying the noun **plays**, and **based on** is the correct phrasal verb.
 
• **and she is really** – This part is a simple conjunction and adverbial phrase that is grammatically sound.
 
• **adept at it** – This part is correct. The adjective **adept** (meaning very skilled or proficient) is correctly followed by the preposition **at**.
</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence:

_______ being in great trouble, he came forward to help me in my need.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**In spite of**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** __ 
• The prepositional phrase **'In spite of'** is used to express **contrast** between two ideas. 
• It means 'notwithstanding' or 'despite'. It is used to show that something happened although something else might have prevented it. 
• In the given sentence, there is a contrast: the subject was in **great trouble** (a negative situation), yet he **helped** (a positive action). 
• The phrase is correctly followed by the **gerund** (being). Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**. **Complete Sentence:** *'**In spite of**__ being in great trouble, he came forward to help me in my need.'* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 1: Due to** is used to indicate a **reason** or **cause**. 
• **Option 2: According to** is used to report what someone else has said or what a source indicates. 
• **Option 4: Owing to** is similar to 'due to' and is used to explain the **reason** for something. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."

The governor assured the media that the crisis was under control and __would be soon overcome by__ the efforts of the administration.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence follows the **sequence of tenses** rule. Since the main verb **assured** is in the **past tense**, the subordinate clause must use the past form of the modal, which is **would**.
 
• The primary improvement required is the **placement of the adverb**. In English grammar, adverbs like **soon** are typically placed after the first auxiliary verb. Therefore, **would soon be** is more natural and grammatically standard than **would be soon**.
 
• The **passive voice** construction **overcome by** is correct here as it indicates the agent or means (the efforts of the administration) responsible for the action.
 
• Thus, the phrase **would soon be overcome by** is the most grammatically accurate replacement.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The governor assured the media that the crisis was under control and **would soon be overcome by** the efforts of the administration.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** Uses **will**, which violates the sequence of tenses (past 'assured' requires 'would'), and the preposition **for** is contextually incorrect.
 
• **Option 3:** Uses **was**, which changes the meaning from a future assurance to a completed past action, and **due to** is less precise than **by** in this passive structure.
 
• **Option 4:** Is incorrect because the adverb placement in the original sentence is awkward and can be improved for better flow.
</ul

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.
S1. The notion has possession of him.
A. "She is my wife's sister," he said, holding the little dog closely.
B. On another morning he told me that Caruso the singer had married a woman who was his sister-in-law.
C. One morning he told me he was a cousin to the man named Cox who at the time when I write is a candidate for the presidency.
D. He cannot draw close to people near at hand so he gets hold of a name out of a newspaper and his mind plays with it.
S2. His grey watery eyes looked appealingly up to me.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph begins with a fixed sentence **S1** that describes a **notion** or a fixation that has taken hold of a character. 
• **Sentence D is the first sentence** to follow because it explains the nature of this notion, clarifying how the character uses names from a **newspaper** to create imaginary connections: 
• 'He cannot draw close to people near at hand so he gets hold of a name out of a **newspaper** and his mind plays with it.' 
• **Sentence C follows** as it provides the first specific instance of this behavior, introduced by the chronological marker **One morning**: 
• 'One morning he told me he was a cousin to the man named **Cox** who at the time when I write is a **candidate for the presidency**.' 
• **Sentence B is the third sentence** as it presents a second example of his fabrications, using the transition **On another morning**: 
• 'On another morning he told me that **Caruso** the singer had married a woman who was his **sister-in-law**.' 
• **Sentence A follows B** directly, providing the character's direct speech that clarifies the **sister-in-law** relationship mentioned previously: 
• ''She is my **wife's sister**,' he said, holding the little dog closely.' 
• The sequence ends with the fixed sentence **S2**, which describes the character's expression (**grey watery eyes**) after making these claims. 
• The correct sequence is **DCBA**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'The notion has possession of him. He cannot draw close to people near at hand so he gets hold of a name out of a newspaper and his mind plays with it. One morning he told me he was a cousin to the man named Cox who at the time when I write is a candidate for the presidency. On another morning he told me that Caruso the singer had married a woman who was his sister-in-law. 'She is my wife's sister,' he said, holding the little dog closely. His grey watery eyes looked appealingly up to me.'</div

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."

It was __a once-in-the-lifetime opportunity__ that many would consider invaluable, but very few got the chance to experience.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**a once-in-a-lifetime**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **once-in-a-lifetime** is a standard **idiomatic expression** and a **compound adjective** used to describe an event that is exceptionally rare, unique, or likely to happen only once.
 
• In the original sentence, the phrase **once-in-the-lifetime** is used. This is grammatically incorrect because the standard idiom requires the **indefinite article** (a) within the hyphenated structure to denote any single lifetime, rather than the **definite article** (the).
 
• Linguistically, the word **once** begins with the vowel letter **o**, but it is phonetically pronounced starting with the **consonant sound** **w** (/wʌns/).
 
• According to **English grammar rules**, the article **a** is used before words that begin with a **consonant sound**, while **an** is reserved for words beginning with a **vowel sound**. Therefore, **a once-in-a-lifetime** is the only phonetically and idiomatically correct choice.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Phonetic Article Selection**:
 
 
• The choice between **a** and **an** depends on the **initial sound** of the next word.
